title: Brewery Merchandise That Sells | Craft Beer School
desc: What brewery merchandise is actually worth stocking in India, what margin to expect, and why most caps and t-shirts sit unsold on a shelf.
teaser: Most brewery merchandise racks are full of stock nobody wanted, ordered in the wrong sizes, in colours that do not match the brand, and forgotten within a month.
standfirst: Merchandise can be a genuine, high margin side of a brewery, or a cupboard full of unsold t-shirts. The difference is almost entirely in what you choose to stock and why.
sections: Start with what people actually wear out of the taproom

A plain cap or a well cut t-shirt with a small, confident logo gets worn in public far more often than a loud design covering the whole chest. Merchandise only markets your brewery when someone wears it somewhere else, so the test for any new item should be whether a regular would wear it to the gym or the market, not just around the taproom on the night they bought it.

Look at what your own staff choose to wear off shift, when nobody is telling them to represent the brand. If they would not pick an item for themselves out of genuine preference, a paying customer is unlikely to either, no matter how good the design looks in a mockup.

Resist the temptation to print every logo variation you own onto a shirt just because the artwork exists. A single confident mark beaten into people's memory works harder than five different designs competing for the same shelf space.
Glassware sells itself if the beer is good

A branded glass, particularly one shaped for a specific style you actually brew, sells consistently because it is functional and because a customer who liked the beer wants to drink it the same way at home. Unlike apparel, glassware has no sizing problem and very little unsold risk if you order a sensible quantity, and it doubles as a quiet reminder of your brand sitting in someone's kitchen cabinet long after the visit.

Keep the shape simple and durable rather than delicate. A glass that survives a dishwasher gets used regularly, and a glass that gets used regularly is advertising that never stops running.
Sizing kills more merchandise budgets than design does

Apparel ordered in the wrong size mix is the single most common reason a merchandise rack sits full for months. Indian sizing charts vary between manufacturers, and a batch skewed toward sizes your regulars do not wear becomes dead stock regardless of how good the design is. Order a small first run and track what actually sells before committing to a large print run, and ask your printer for their actual measurements rather than trusting a generic size chart, and keep a simple record of what sold in which size so the next order is informed rather than a repeat guess.
Price it as merchandise, not as a discount on beer

Merchandise should carry a healthy margin because it is not the core product, and pricing it too low to move stock quickly usually signals cheapness rather than value. A well made item priced fairly, even if it takes longer to sell through, does more for the brand than a pile of underpriced stock nobody remembers buying a year later.

If an item is not selling at a fair price, the problem is usually the design or the relevance, not the price. Fix that before discounting it into a clearance bin near the door, which trains regulars to wait for a markdown instead of buying at full price.
Sell it where the story already lives

Merchandise moves best at events and at the point where someone is already having a good experience, rather than sitting untouched on a shelf near the door. Our taproom events guide covers how a recurring event creates exactly that moment, and pairing a new merchandise drop with a launch, as in our launch guide, gives regulars two reasons to show up rather than one, which matters more for long-term loyalty than any discount ever will, and costs the brewery nothing extra to arrange.
Treat it as branding, not as a revenue line

For most breweries, merchandise will never be a significant share of revenue, and treating it as one leads to over-ordering stock that then sits in a storeroom for years. Its real value is as walking advertising and as a way for a loyal customer to show allegiance to a brand they like, which matters for word of mouth in a category where most other advertising is restricted. See our brand positioning guide for how merchandise should reflect the position you have already chosen, rather than becoming a separate, disconnected product line that confuses regulars about what the brand actually stands for.
faqs: What sells best in a brewery taproom?
Caps, well fitted t-shirts and branded glassware are the most reliable sellers. Anything loud, oversized in the wrong sizes, or unrelated to actually drinking the beer tends to sit unsold.
How much merchandise should a small brewery order to start?
A small first run in a limited size range, tracked closely for what actually sells, is safer than a large order based on a guess. Reorder based on real data, not on what looks good in a mockup.
Should merchandise be cheap to move quickly?
No. Underpricing signals cheapness rather than value. Price it fairly and expect it to sell more slowly than beer, because that is normal for a side product.
